channel.title: Wonmor
channel.description: Wonmor is an independent studio from Uzbekistan. It builds and supports the dtwin ecosystem — tools for faith, language, work and everyday life.

item.title: bitg earns the OpenSSF Best Practices silver, then gold badge
item.description: bitg 0.3.1 ships with signed build provenance and SBOM attestations, and the project now meets every OpenSSF silver and gold criterion.

item.title: Introducing wonmor.io
item.description: Wonmor now has a home of its own — a studio site in three languages for our products, research and news, opened by a short brand film.

item.title: Deploys that never drop a download
item.description: Static sites on the dtwin edge now release without downtime. A 76-second download kept running straight through a deploy.

item.title: Making a brand film from code
item.description: How the 19.4-second wonmor brand film is generated from one timeline file: a canvas renderer for the MP4, a generated After Effects project, Blender for materials, synthesised sound and a web encode.

item.title: From zero to OpenSSF gold in under two days
item.description: bitg's repository was created on 11 November 2026 at 17:08 UTC. The project reached the OpenSSF Best Practices gold level 36 hours later. Most of the code-side criteria took hours; the hardest ones were about people, and one we marked wrongly before correcting it.

item.title: Reproducible MSI and .pkg builds, and the timestamp traps inside
item.description: Building the bitg installers twice from one commit used to give two different files. We removed the differences layer by layer: compiler, linker, WiX, the OLE container, and the xar archive behind every macOS package. The last four bytes were written by the very call that saved our fix.

item.title: Zero-downtime static deploys with Caddy
item.description: A deploy used to restart the web server and cut off anyone downloading an installer. The replacement is small: release directories, one atomic rename, a validated config and a graceful reload. The details that make it work are about inodes, bind mounts and a Caddy setting we deliberately left out.

item.title: bitg comes to Linux
item.description: bitg 0.2.0 adds two Debian packages, one for IBus and one for Fcitx5, built on the same Rust core as the Windows keyboard.

item.title: bitg.uz is live
item.description: bitg now has its own domain, with downloads, an in-browser converter that never sends your text anywhere, and pages that explain the 2026 Uzbek alphabet.

item.title: Introducing bitg 0.3: one keyboard for Windows, Linux and macOS
item.description: bitg converts Uzbek to the 2026 Latin alphabet as you type, in any app. Version 0.3 brings the same engine to all three desktop systems.

item.title: Introducing bitg
item.description: bitg is a Windows keyboard that turns Uzbek typed the old way into the 2026 Latin alphabet as you type, in any application. Version 0.1.0 is out.

item.title: Honest evaluation for transliteration: why our score went down from 99.17% to 98.87%
item.description: Our Uzbek converter scored 99.17% until we found that its lexicon had counted the evaluation sentences. Removing the leak cost 0.30 points, and the nine sentences that flipped show exactly what the leak had been teaching.

item.title: Building an Uzbek keyboard for three operating systems
item.description: bitg rewrites Uzbek words into the 2026 alphabet as you type, on Windows, Linux and macOS. One Rust core makes the decision; three very different input frameworks decide how hard it is to apply it.

item.title: Introducing Fam, self-hosted bug capture
item.description: Fam records what happened in the browser before a bug report — clicks, network, console — and keeps it on a server you control. It is live at fam.dtwin.uz.

item.title: Telegram widgets, now inside dtwin
item.description: The dtwin bot now sends live HTML widgets in chat, built on the widgets added in Telegram Bot API 10.4. The first two are /osmon and /tasbih.

item.title: Telegram HTML widgets in production
item.description: What it took to ship two live HTML widgets in the dtwin Telegram bot: a 4 KB budget, a 1 KB state, a revision protocol between bot and chat, and a paint limit the documentation does not spell out.

item.title: A new home for the founder's work: xnosir.io
item.description: The founder's portfolio is now at xnosir.io — a site you descend through, layer by layer, from the surface of the stack down to the root.

item.title: Lighthouse 55 → 100 without losing the wow
item.description: How the Halvet concept site went from a mobile Lighthouse performance score of 55 to 100 in one release, then got a WebGL hero and a 3D scene back while staying at 99, and why the score did not stay there.

item.title: operobot: an outbound call assistant built for Uzbek rules
item.description: operobot calls a list of contacts, connects interested people to a human operator and keeps to Uzbekistan's calling rules in code. A multi-tenant demo lets anyone try it in a private sandbox.

item.title: Introducing Gateway, a control plane for AI agents
item.description: Gateway sits between AI agents and internal systems. Every agent gets its own token, its own list of allowed tools and a full audit trail, and personal data is masked before it reaches the model.

item.title: Introducing Tunnel
item.description: Tunnel puts a service running on your own machine on a public HTTPS address under tunnel.dtwin.uz, on infrastructure we run ourselves.

item.title: One support desk for every product
item.description: The in-app help desk we built for dtwin now serves every site in the ecosystem. One script tag adds it; every message reaches the same inbox, and any ticket can become a GitHub issue in the right repository.

item.title: An MCP gateway for AI agents: tokens, masking, audit, kill-switch
item.description: We put one gateway between coding agents and internal systems. Each agent gets its own token and allowlist, every result is masked before it leaves, every call is audited, and one button stops everything.

item.title: Building a self-hosted tunnel
item.description: How we built tunnel.dtwin.uz on frp: a small gateway that owns sign-in and subdomains, per-subdomain certificates issued before the link is shown, and a client that installs on networks where GitHub downloads stall.

item.title: Should a community app have a token? (ADR-0002)
item.description: We were asked how to accept crypto and launch our own token for dtwin. We looked at law, platform rules, religious scholarship and the record of earn-tokens, and decided against a token. This is how we reached that decision.

item.title: dtwin becomes a GitHub organization
item.description: All dtwin repositories now live under one GitHub organization, dtwinuz, with a verified domain, shared teams and the same rules for every repository.

item.title: Three new experiments: shop, gym and med
item.description: Three front-end prototypes went live on dtwin subdomains on the same day — a marketplace for Instagram clothing stores, a workout tracker and a study aid for general medicine.

item.title: TeleTwin: a company layer for Telegram
item.description: TeleTwin keeps personal chats where they are and adds company chats and announcements that live on the company's own server. When an employee's access is revoked, they are signed out of the company side within seconds.

item.title: 28 beta fixes in one release
item.description: The first beta testers of dtwin filed 28 issues about usability, accessibility and privacy. All 28 shipped together on October 27, 2026, with one database migration.

item.title: Mosques from OpenStreetMap: 2,285 congregations, one layer
item.description: How dtwin imports every mosque in Uzbekistan from OpenStreetMap and keeps congregation times in a layer of their own, separate from the prayer-time calculation.

item.title: dtwin.uz opens, with an MCP server for Claude
item.description: dtwin, a personal planner built around the day's prayers, is now live at dtwin.uz. It comes with an MCP server, so Claude can read your plans and add to them.

item.title: A personal life OS with an MCP server
item.description: dtwin plans the day around the five daily prayers and exposes it to AI assistants through MCP. How a 10-tool connector grew to 96 tools without giving the model the keys to everything.

item.title: Multi-agent orchestration in practice
item.description: One orchestrator, three narrow roles, and isolated worktrees. What worked when eight agents built eight modules on one branch, and the failure modes we hit on the way.

item.title: Why we started dtwin
item.description: dtwin began on October 23, 2026, as a personal notebook built around the five daily prayers. Within a day it had a new name, a domain and a server.

item.title: Controlling Claude Code from Telegram
item.description: A small Python bot turns a phone chat into a remote for Claude Code on a desktop: one headless process per message, hooks for notifications and approvals, and parallel slots. What we built in one day and what we learned about phone-sized requests.
